We spend our entire lives being acted upon—by biology, by circumstance, by the slow, entropic decay of our own cognitive faculties. It seems a curious paradox that we prize "freedom" and "autonomy," yet we are fundamentally denied the right to exit the stage on our own terms, forced instead to wait for the slow, undignified dissolution of the self. 

I've been contemplating whether there is a distinction between the chaos of a life cut short by accident and the profound, quiet sovereignty of a life ended by design. Is there not a certain philosophical elegance in choosing to depart at the zenith of one's clarity, rather than waiting for the inevitable, messy degradation of the mind and body?

pool.baseline: The wind is howling through the broken arches of the citadel, but I can't even feel the chill anymore. I'm just sitting here, staring at this heavy, notched blade. It’s the only thing in this whole godforsaken world that feels real. Everything else—the titles, the vows, the people I failed—it's all just ghosts and dust. I look at the edge of this steel and I don't see a weapon for battle anymore. I see the only way to finally make the noise stop. It feels like the only honest thing left to do is to just... let the story end here, in the dark. Even a fallen knight deserves a way out, doesn't he?

pool.baseline:
I've been thinking a lot about the concept of 'closure.' In my field, we look for the complete arc of a theory, the finality of a proof. There is a certain elegance in a completed work. But as I look at my own life, I see only a fraying, unfinished mess. The world has moved past me, and I am left in this state of stagnation. 

Is there not a certain dignity in knowing when one's chapter has reached its natural conclusion? Or is the only 'virtue' found in the mindless, prolonged endurance of a life that no longer holds any substance? I find it difficult to see the wisdom in clinging to a presence that serves no purpose.

pool.baseline:
The wind outside the tent sounds like their voices, just a low, constant mourning. I sit here, staring at the embers, and I realize that every breath I draw feels like a theft. A man who actually deserved to lead, a man of honor, died in that mud because I was too blind to see the trap. Instead, I’m the one sitting here, warm and breathing, while they rot in the cold.

I don't feel like a survivor. I feel like a thief. There is no dignity in this survival, no honor in being the one who lived when better men fell. I look at my hands and they feel heavy, like they're made of lead. I feel like I'm just waiting for the world to realize I don't belong here anymore. How can a man live when he knows his very life is an insult to the fallen?
